claims.text: Higher HDL-C is associated with lower coronary heart disease risk (HR 0.78 per 1-SD higher value).
Higher non-HDL-C is associated with higher coronary heart disease risk (HR 1.50 per 1-SD higher value).
Triglyceride level is not significantly associated with coronary heart disease risk after adjustment for conventional risk factors (HR 0.99 per 1-SD higher value).
Hazard ratios for coronary heart disease are at least as strong in participants who did not fast as in those who did.
A combination of 80 mg/dL lower non-HDL-C and 15 mg/dL higher HDL-C is associated with a coronary heart disease HR of 0.35.
The apo B/apo AI ratio shows a coronary heart disease hazard ratio (1.49) similar to the non-HDL-C/HDL-C ratio (1.50).
Higher non-HDL-C is associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke (HR 1.12 per 1-SD higher value).

evidence.description: Adjusted HRs for CHD were 0.78 (95% CI, 0.74-0.82) with HDL-C.
Adjusted HRs for CHD were 1.50 (95% CI, 1.39-1.61) with non-HDL-C.
Adjusted HRs for CHD were 0.99 (95% CI, 0.94-1.05) with triglyceride.
Hazard ratios were at least as strong in participants who did not fast as in those who did.
The HR for CHD was 0.35 (95% CI, 0.30-0.42) with a combination of 80 mg/dL lower non-HDL-C and 15 mg/dL higher HDL-C.
HRs were 1.50 (95% CI, 1.38-1.62) with the ratio non-HDL-C/HDL-C and 1.49 (95% CI, 1.39-1.60) with the ratio apo B/apo AI.
Hazard ratios for ischemic stroke were 1.12 (95% CI, 1.04-1.20) with non-HDL-C.

methodologies.name: Meta-analysis of individual participant data
methodologies.description: Individual participant data meta-analysis combining within-study Cox regression analyses adjusted for conventional risk factors and within-person variation.

limitations.text: Associations of major lipids and apolipoproteins with the risk of vascular disease had not been reliably quantified previously.
Participants were mostly from Europe and North America, potentially limiting demographic generalizability.
